title: ICMR-NIN's Dietary Framework Tackles India's Dual Burden of Malnutrition and Obesity
excerpt: India's national nutrition body has issued comprehensive guidelines addressing both undernutrition and rising obesity, recommending foods from eight groups and warning against ultra-processed products.
body:
• ICMR-NIN's dietary guidelines address India's dual burden of undernutrition and obesity through a two-axis classification framework
  • The guidelines recommend deriving nutrients from at least eight food groups daily, with vegetables, fruits, roots, and tubers making up half of daily intake
  • Research shows 56.4% of India's total disease burden is attributable to unhealthy diets
  • Experts are calling for expanded guidelines that include food safety, mental health nutrition, and sustainable eating recommendations

India's Double Challenge

India faces a nutritional paradox that few countries confront at the same scale: widespread undernutrition alongside rapidly rising rates of obesity and diet-related chronic disease. The Indian Council of Medical Research and the National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) have responded with a dual-axis dietary framework — one that simultaneously addresses nutrient deficiency and dietary excess.

Research published in the Journal of the Epidemiology Foundation of India describes the 2024 ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines as a comprehensive framework to address what scientists call the "dual burden of malnutrition." The guidelines emphasize balanced diets, physical activity, and the consumption of diverse, nutrient-rich foods across all life stages.

The stakes are substantial: new estimates cited by ICMR-NIN show that 56.4% of the total disease burden in India is attributable to unhealthy diets. Food systems are also responsible for approximately one-third of greenhouse gas emissions, making sustainable eating a dual health-and-climate imperative.

The Eight Food Groups

At the core of the ICMR-NIN approach is the "My Plate" recommendation, which prescribes a daily diet drawn from at least eight food groups. According to the NIN's published guidelines, vegetables, fruits, roots, and tubers should compose approximately half of daily food intake. The remaining portion should consist of cereals, millets, pulses, flesh foods, eggs, nuts, oil seeds, and milk or curd.

For a standard 2,000-calorie diet, the guidelines specify: 260 grams of cereals including nutri-cereals, 85 grams of pulses, 300 ml of milk or curd, 400 grams of vegetables including green leafy vegetables, 100 grams of fruits, 30 grams of nuts and seeds, and 27 grams of fats and oils.

"Sustainable eating helps address the problems with our food systems, by consuming foods that are produced in an economically, socially, and environmentally responsible manner."

— ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines

Vegetarians face particular challenges in meeting requirements for vitamin B12 and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. The guidelines recommend flax seeds, chia seeds, and other plant sources to bridge these gaps.

Ultra-Processed Foods Under Scrutiny

The ICMR-NIN guidelines take a firm position against ultra-processed and packaged foods — a stance that places India alongside a growing global movement to restrict these products. The guidelines were developed by a diverse team of specialists under the direction of Dr. Hemalatha R, director of ICMR-NIN.

The framework issued 17 specific dietary recommendations designed to meet essential nutrient requirements while preventing non-communicable diseases such as obesity and diabetes. The recommendations also advocate for healthy eating habits and lifestyles aligned with India's diverse regional food traditions.

Expanding the Framework

Researchers have called for the guidelines to go further. A commentary in the Journal of the Epidemiology Foundation of India suggests expanding the framework to include specific recommendations on food safety, mental health nutrition, plant-based and sustainable eating, digital nutrition tools, and fortified foods.

"Integrating these aspects could make the guidelines more relevant, equipping individuals and policymakers with actionable strategies to address India's evolving public health challenges."

— K. Madan Gopal et al., National Health Systems Resource Centre

The Indian Food Composition Tables, maintained by NIN since 1971 and last updated in 2017, provide nutritional data for 528 raw food items across 20 food groups. An app version has been developed to make this data accessible to consumers.

For the Indian diaspora, the ICMR-NIN framework offers a scientifically grounded alternative to Western dietary guidelines, rooted in India's food diversity and tailored to South Asian metabolic profiles — relevant for communities worldwide navigating health risks that disproportionately affect people of Indian origin.
